issues.description: Nil/zero-guard boilerplate is duplicated across ~20 accessors instead of captured in one helper
issues.detail: The same `var s []T; if f != nil { s = f.field }; return seq.NewFixedSlice(s, ...)` pattern is copy-pasted across ir_file.go, ir_type.go, ir_imports.go, and ir_member.go. A single helper (e.g. nil-tolerant seq.NewFixedSlice or a sliceOrNil filter) would state the invariant once and let every future accessor inherit it.

issues.description: Two parallel nil-zero idioms coexist (`f == nil` vs `IsZero()`); pick one canonical predicate
issues.detail: *File guards with `f == nil` while value types (Type, Member, Oneof, Element) guard with `!x.IsZero()`. Both express the same abstract notion of absence but force maintainers to remember which type uses which. Define IsZero on *File too, or route every accessor through a shared guarded helper, so the rule is one line of prose.

issues.description: Zero-value contract is implicit; the panic-free invariant should be stated, not only enforced by reflection
issues.detail: The PR establishes a real ADT promise — every accessor on a zero/nil receiver returns the zero value of its result type — but that contract appears nowhere in package docs. State it once (e.g. on doc.go or IsZero) so future authors know the precondition is `none` and the reflective test is a backstop rather than the spec.

issues.description: ValueNodeIndex returns -1 as an in-band sentinel, complicating callers and inviting an At(-1) panic
issues.detail: Element.ValueNodeIndex now returns -1 on the zero value. Every other zero accessor returns the type's zero, so callers doing `MessageKeys().At(e.ValueNodeIndex())` will index by -1 and panic — the failure has merely moved. Return `(int, bool)` or add a HasValueNode predicate so presence and value are separate.

issues.description: Reflection-driven zero test is too clever and silently skips methods that take arguments
issues.detail: testZeroAny filters to NumIn==1, treats any return with a Len method as a container, and special-cases IsZero/Context/ValueNodeIndex by name. Accessors taking arguments (e.g. ImportFor) are never exercised, and future return types with unrelated Len semantics will silently pass. A boring per-type table of (name, accessor) would be longer but durable.

issues.description: imports.Transitive/Directs rely on unstated invariants that one refactor could re-break
issues.detail: Transitive uses `files[:max(0, len(files)-1)]` to drop the implicit descriptor.proto, and Directs's closure still captures `i.publicEnd` etc. — safe only because an empty slice short-circuits the mapper. The invariants ('last element is descriptor.proto', 'nil receiver yields empty slice so closure never runs') are documented nowhere; state them or refactor so the guard is explicit.

synthesis.summary: The panel agrees the PR fixes real panics on zero/nil IR values and that the reflective zero-test is a valuable structural backstop, but the shape of the fix is wrong: the same defensive guard is copy-pasted across ~20 accessors instead of captured in one helper, and two parallel idioms (`f == nil` vs `IsZero()`) now coexist in the same package. The zero-value contract is implicit — only the test states it — and should be written down in package docs. ValueNodeIndex's `-1` sentinel is a small but real abstraction leak that has merely relocated the panic to any caller that indexes with it. The reflection-driven test is clever in the bad way: it silently skips methods with arguments and leans on name-based special cases where a small explicit table would be more durable. Net verdict: correct in intent, under-factored in execution; land with follow-ups, not as-is.
